title: The Exchange Changed the Contract in January; the Regulator Voted Not To Act in March: Two Records of the Silver Corner
participants: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
Dan M. Berkovitz, CFTC General Counsel

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Not quantified by either source. The Commission's chronology records no position size, no price and no profit; its General Counsel's later testimony names the episode — "the Hunt Silver Crisis in 1979-1980" — without sizing it. Any figure for what the corner was worth is outside what was read.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Two structural facts, one from each record. From the chronology: speculative position limits existed contract by contract, not across the board — the universal requirement, Regulation 1.61, arrived on 16 October 1981, nineteen months after the collapse. From the testimony: in a futures contract, position size, margin and the right to trade at all are the exchange's to set, and can be reset while a position is open — which is what COMEX did.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The regulator's knowledge is on the record: "April 28, 1977—The CFTC asks the U.S. District Court in Chicago to order seven members of the Hunt family of Dallas, and a related company, to liquidate positions that exceed the three million bushel speculative position limit for soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade." Three years before silver, the agency had identified the same actors exceeding a position limit and asked a court to make them unwind. Then the exchange moved first, and privately to its own members' advantage: "As a result of the Hunt Silver Crisis in 1979-1980, the COMEX under emergency authority imposed speculative position limits on the silver futures contract on January 7, 1980."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The exchange, not the regulator, turned the market. In the Commission's own later account: "Then, on January 21, COMEX suspended trading in silver and announced that it would only accept liquidation orders. The price of silver began to decline." A market in which the only permitted order is a sale has one direction left — and the members of the exchange that made the rule were the other side of the position it broke. Two months later, as the price went: "March 28, 1980—After careful consideration of a host of market factors, the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." It had used those powers freely for grain in January over a policy announcement; it declined them for silver in March as the market collapsed.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The sequence afterwards made the exchange's emergency terms permanent and deferred the question of fault. "On April 4, 1980, the CFTC approved speculative position limits for the silver futures contract. These limits at the COMEX were set at 500 contracts for the spot/next month and 2,000 contracts" otherwise. A report to Congress followed on 29 May 1981, "as required by Public Law 96-276"; Regulation 1.61 requiring position limits in all futures contracts on 16 October 1981; and the charge almost five years after the collapse — "February 28, 1985—The CFTC ends its silver investigation, alleging that Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt, and other individuals and firms manipulated and attempted to manipulate silver prices in 1979 and 1980." Alleging. This dossier does not convert the agency's own word into a finding, and the outcome of that action was not read.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The CFTC's emergency powers under the Commodity Exchange Act, which the agency had exercised and a court had just upheld — the CBOT March wheat contract closed in March 1979, "the first time the Commission orders a market closed in the interest of preventing a price manipulation", and the Seventh Circuit affirming the emergency authority in September 1979 — alongside an exchange's own emergency authority over its contract's size, margin and tradability.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Permanent federal speculative position limits on silver, approved on 4 April 1980 at 500 and 2,000 contracts — the exchange's January emergency terms adopted by the regulator — and, in October 1981, Regulation 1.61, now part of 17 CFR 150, requiring speculative position limits in all futures contracts.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A position is built against the members of an exchange; the exchange, using its own emergency authority, restricts the contract and then permits only liquidation, and the price moves the way the restriction points; the federal regulator, which has the power and has just used it elsewhere, declines to intervene as the price falls; and then it makes the exchange's emergency terms the standing rule for the next corner — so the rule that ended this one is written by the party it was held against.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Two decoys, pointing opposite ways. One: that the regulators and the exchanges conspired to change the rules on "Silver Thursday" and break the Hunt brothers' corner. The other: that the Hunts were simply beaten by the market, which corrected their attempt.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Both fail, and the two records read for this dossier fail them separately. The "beaten by the market" version fails on the Commission's own later account of the exchange: COMEX "under emergency authority imposed speculative position limits on the silver futures contract on January 7, 1980", and "on January 21, COMEX suspended trading in silver and announced that it would only accept liquidation orders. The price of silver began to decline." The correction followed the rule change, and the rule was made by the exchange whose members held the other side. The "regulators conspired" version fails on the Commission's own chronology: on 28 March 1980, as silver collapsed, "the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." The federal regulator declined — having closed a wheat contract in March 1979 to prevent a manipulation, had its emergency authority affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in September 1979, suspended five grain markets for two days in January 1980 over the Soviet embargo, and sued these same traders over position limits in 1977. So the record supports neither a market correction nor a regulatory conspiracy. It supports an exchange acting in its members' interest under its own emergency authority, a regulator with the power choosing not to use it, and then the regulator adopting the exchange's emergency terms as permanent law — on 4 April 1980 for silver, and for every futures contract in October 1981 — before alleging manipulation four years and eleven months after the collapse. ON SOURCING: the two CFTC history pages were read here in a browser (cftc.gov returns 403 to scripts). The General Counsel's 2010 testimony and the 2013 Federal Register rulemaking were fetched and verified on a parallel branch through glm-recheck --strict-sources and are carried in at the merge with that stated in each citation; on 18 October 2026 the testimony page was confirmed in a browser to be what the citation says and the Federal Register PDF was confirmed to be served, but neither body was re-read here. No underlying order, complaint or court opinion was read by either session, the 1981 report to Congress was not located, and nothing read establishes what positions the Hunts held, how large the corner was, who lost money, or how the 1985 action ended.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's own published chronology, 1970s and 1980s pages, recording: the 28 April 1977 court action to make seven members of the Hunt family liquidate soybean positions exceeding the three-million-bushel limit on the Chicago Board of Trade; the 4 January 1979 moratorium on gold and silver leverage contracts; the 16 March 1979 closure of the CBOT March wheat contract, the first market closed to prevent price manipulation; the 12 September 1979 Seventh Circuit affirmance of the emergency power; the 6 January 1980 two-day suspension of five agricultural contracts after the Soviet grain embargo; the 28 March 1980 vote, "after careful consideration of a host of market factors", not to use emergency powers to suspend silver futures as prices plummeted; the 29 May 1981 report to Congress under Public Law 96-276; the 16 October 1981 adoption of Regulation 1.61 requiring speculative position limits in all futures contracts; the 28 September 1984 study of futures trading by persons possessing material nonpublic information; and the 28 February 1985 end of the silver investigation, alleging manipulation by Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt and others in 1979 and 1980. The testimony of CFTC General Counsel Dan M. Berkovitz of 25 March 2010, as verified on a parallel branch: that as a result of the Hunt Silver Crisis COMEX under emergency authority imposed speculative position limits on silver futures on 7 January 1980, and that on 4 April 1980 the CFTC approved speculative position limits for the contract at 500 contracts for the spot/next month and 2,000 otherwise. The Commission's 2013 Federal Register rulemaking on position limits, as verified on the same branch: that on 21 January 1980 COMEX suspended trading in silver, announced it would accept only liquidation orders, and the price of silver began to decline.

citations.quoteOrFact: Read on the Commission's own site. ACCESS NOTE: cftc.gov serves a bot-verification interstitial to scripted requests and returns HTTP 403 to them, so automated link checks will report this URL as blocked; it was opened and read in a browser. THIS IS THE AGENCY'S OWN DATED CHRONOLOGY, not a narrative account, and three of its entries establish that the Commission had the power, had used it, and had already been to court about this family. ON THE HUNTS, THREE YEARS BEFORE THE SILVER CORNER: "April 28, 1977—The CFTC asks the U.S. District Court in Chicago to order seven members of the Hunt family of Dallas, and a related company, to liquidate positions that exceed the three million bushel speculative position limit for soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade." ON THE POWER, EXERCISED: "March 16, 1979—In an emergency action, the CFTC votes to prohibit further trading in the Chicago Board of Trade March wheat futures contract, the first time the Commission orders a market closed in the interest of preventing a price manipulation." ON THE POWER, CONFIRMED BY A COURT MONTHS BEFORE THE SILVER PEAK: "September 12, 1979—The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirms the CFTC's authority to act during market emergencies, and concludes that judicial review of the Commission's determination of such an emergency would thwart the purpose for which Congress granted the CFTC emergency powers." Also recorded: "January 4, 1979—The CFTC announces a temporary moratorium on entry into the leverage contract business in gold and silver bullion and bulk coins." WHAT A CHRONOLOGY CANNOT DO: these are the agency's own one-sentence summaries of its own actions. No underlying order, complaint, court opinion or report was read for this dossier. The 1977 soybean action's outcome is not stated here and is not asserted; nothing here says what positions the Hunts held in silver, when, or through whom.

citations.quoteOrFact: Read on the Commission's own site; cftc.gov returns HTTP 403 with a bot-verification interstitial to scripted requests, so link checks report it blocked. It was opened and read in a browser. THE DECISION NOT TO ACT, ON THE DAY: "March 28, 1980—After careful consideration of a host of market factors, the CFTC votes not to use its emergency powers to order a suspension of trading in silver futures as prices plummet." Set against the 1970s chronology — a market closed on wheat in March 1979 to prevent manipulation, and the Seventh Circuit affirming the emergency power in September 1979 — this is a deliberate non-use of a power the Commission had just established it possessed. Note also what it did do that year, for a different commodity and a different reason: "January 6, 1980—In an emergency action, the CFTC orders the suspension of futures trading for two days for wheat, corn, oats, soybean meal, and soybean oil on four exchanges after President Carter announces an embargo on the sale of certain agricultural goods to the Soviet Union." Grain markets were suspended in January for a policy announcement; silver was not suspended in March as it collapsed. THE REPORT, FOURTEEN MONTHS LATER: "May 29, 1981—As required by Public Law 96-276, the CFTC transmits to Congress a report on events in the silver market during late 1979 and early 1980, and on issues involving futures contracts on financial instruments." (That report was not located or read.) THE RULE, NINETEEN MONTHS LATER: "October 16, 1981—The CFTC adopts Regulation 1.61 (now part of CFTC Regulation 150, 17 CFR 150) requiring exchanges to establish speculative position limits in all futures contracts." THE ALLEGATION, ALMOST FIVE YEARS LATER: "February 28, 1985—The CFTC ends its silver investigation, alleging that Nelson Bunker Hunt, William Herbert Hunt, and other individuals and firms manipulated and attempted to manipulate silver prices in 1979 and 1980." ALLEGING — the Commission's own word, in its own chronology, and this dossier does not convert it into a finding. AND ONE ENTRY THAT DESCRIBES THIS ATLAS'S SUBJECT IN THE REGULATOR'S OWN TITLE: "September 28, 1984—The CFTC submits 'A Study of the Nature, Extent and Effects of Futures Trading by Persons Possessing Material, Nonpublic Information' to its Congressional oversight committees." That study was not located or read either, and nothing is asserted about its contents.
